claims.text: Approximately 5 vol% diamond nanoplatelets will be incorporated and aligned within the copper phase of a W–Cu composite.
The aligned diamond nanoplatelets will form bridging networks within the copper phase.
The aligned diamond nanoplatelets will form bridging networks at the Cu–W interface.
These nanoplatelet networks will enhance heat-transfer paths through the composite.
Diamond has extremely high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Well-dispersed and aligned diamond nanoplatelets will lower thermal boundary resistance between copper and tungsten.
Adequate metal–diamond interfacial bonding can be achieved.
Lower interfacial resistance and diamond-mediated heat-transfer paths will improve heat dissipation in W–Cu.
The inherent mechanical robustness and irradiation resistance of tungsten will be preserved after adding diamond nanoplatelets.
Adding aligned diamond nanoplatelets will preserve the composite's irradiation resistance.
Adding aligned diamond nanoplatelets will preserve the composite's mechanical durability.
The modified composite will have at least about 15–20% higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable unmodified W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will exhibit no significant degradation in mechanical strength relative to the baseline.
The modified composite will exhibit no significant degradation in irradiation resistance relative to the baseline.
The predicted benefit will hold under high thermal flux, temperatures up to about 1500 °C, and fusion-relevant irradiation doses.
Poor alignment, significant interfacial mismatch, or excessive diamond content may compromise mechanical integrity or cause operating-condition thermal stress.
High copper concentrations can reduce ductility and promote brittle fracture in a diamond-compatible CoCrCuxFeNi binder system.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome permits any degradation that is not significant, whereas the falsification rule treats any measurable degradation in mechanical or irradiation performance as falsifying. A small measurable but statistically insignificant degradation would therefore be both permitted and disqualifying.
